frameworks.name: Work Exponentially to Compound Returns
frameworks.definition: Absolute work shows diminishing returns, but relative excellence (being #1 vs #2) produces exponential payoff gains; 10x work input yields outsized returns in competitive markets.

frameworks.name: Counting in Hundreds Framework
frameworks.definition: Measure work effort in hundreds of hours per project to achieve genuine depth of understanding and quality; work expands to fill time allowed, but quality threshold is reached only at extreme hour counts.

claims.text: Working 100x harder than baseline competitors produces disproportionate (million-times) payoff because relative position—being #1 instead of #2—compounds exponentially in markets, even though absolute work hours show diminishing returns. Alex Hormozi illustrates this via Olympic racing: a 10x effort increase yields gold (not silver), translating to market gaps like Uber vs Lyft (10x size difference).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: First place captures disproportionate market share and valuation relative to second place; the effort delta (10x) translates to outcome delta (10x+) because market rewards scarcity and dominance.
bounded_by: Does not apply in cooperative or non-ranked contexts
Assumes market structure rewards relative position (winner-take-most, not commodities)

claims.text: Hormozi's standards for finished work have continuously risen over time; early presentations (19 slides, 4 bullets each, 8 hours total) now seem embarrassing compared to current standards. He now counts work effort in hundreds of hours per project, not hours, recognizing that depth of understanding only emerges at extreme time investments.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to high-stakes creative/strategic work (presentations, books, video editing)

numbers.axis: work hours per project over career progression

anchors.value: hundreds of hours per project (e.g., book: 19 drafts, 4 full rewrites, 106 hand-drawn images)

bounded_by: Early judgment of time-well-spent was incorrect; only maturity reveals true scope

claims.text: Work does expand to fill available time, but Hormozi's definition of completion is when nothing else can be done to improve it—no removable content, no unclear passages, no missing elements. For his book, this meant 19 drafts, 4 full rewrites, third-grade reading level, and 106 hand-drawn illustrations with the end result being 'if it does not succeed, that's fine. But it will not be for lack of effort.'
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to high-stakes single output (book, core presentation, major deliverable)
bounded_by: Does not apply to low-stakes iterative work where diminishing returns kick in quickly
Assumes single high-impact output, not ongoing production

claims.text: Most people vastly underestimate how much they can actually work. The constraint is not physical capacity but perception of capacity—people think they know their ceiling until they genuinely push beyond it. Hormozi frames his principle as 'I will not be the reason this [work] is not good,' shifting accountability from external limits to personal standards.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to individuals with high personal standards
assumes access to the work to iterate on
bounded_by: Does not account for external constraints (illness, family emergency, resource scarcity)

claims.text: When tasked with editing a video clip, each successive time-block allocation (30 min, 30 min, 30 min, 2 hours, 2 hours, 2 weeks) yields continuous improvement. The 2-week allocation produces qualitatively different output because the executor approaches the problem differently (e.g., full restructure) than compressed timeframes allow.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: creative work where restructuring/reimagining is valuable
executor has genuine capability to improve (not hitting skill ceiling)
claims.mechanism: Longer time horizons permit systems-level thinking and restructuring, not just surface polish; editing quality compounds with time as options expand.

numbers.axis: video editing time allocation and outcome improvement

bounded_by: Assumes the executor has genuine capability improvements, not just opinion changes
Does not apply if output is already optimal for the use case

examples.text: Hormozi's early presentations (19 slides, 4 bullets per slide) took a full 8-hour day to create and he was proud of that effort. Looking back now, he finds them embarrassing. This illustrates how standards compound over a career: what felt like maximum effort at the time was actually bare minimum by later professional standards.

Hormozi completed a book by iterating through 19 total drafts and 4 full rewrites, eventually rewriting the entire manuscript at a third-grade reading level and adding 106 hand-drawn illustrations. He reports that the final version removed every possible weak element and clarified every remaining passage. His standard for completion was: 'I can't take anything else out and I can't add anything to it and I can't make anything clear.'

A team member tasked with editing a short video clip asked if 30 minutes was enough. Hormozi returned it and asked for another 30 minutes of refinement. This repeated until the member was given 2 weeks. At the 2-week mark, the member reported they would 'totally approach it differently' and 'restructure the whole thing,' demonstrating that time horizons unlock different quality levels and strategic approaches.

practices.text: Count work effort in hundreds of hours per major project, not hours. When considering whether something deserves more work, ask 'how many hundreds of hours have I invested?' rather than days or weeks.
Adopt the standard 'I will not be the reason this is not good' for high-stakes deliverables, making yourself accountable for quality regardless of external resource constraints.
Define work completion not by time spent or task checklist, but by the inability to improve further—when nothing can be removed, added, or clarified without degradation.
Apply time-expansion thinking to creative work: allocate extended time horizons (weeks, not days) to unlock restructuring and systems-level improvements beyond surface polish.
